overall: The AG found no Open Meeting Law violation on any of the four allegations across two complaints about the Board's December 19, 2022 and January 9, 2023 meetings; no remedy was ordered.

allegations.summary: Complainant alleged the Dec. 19, 2022 notice was too vague and the Board discussed a Treasurer request to borrow $100,000 from the Stabilization Fund that was not listed.
allegations.key_passage: Here, we find no indication that the Chair anticipated the Treasurer’s requested transfer from the Stabilization Fund, and find no violation of the Open Meeting Law.

allegations.summary: Complainant alleged the Dec. 19, 2022 minutes were insufficient because they did not explain why prior minutes were held or the purpose of the requested fund transfer.
allegations.key_passage: Instead, the Law requires that meeting minutes accurately summarize what was actually discussed.

allegations.summary: Complainant alleged the Jan. 9, 2023 notice was too vague and the Board discussed a business's request to appear about a host community agreement, which was not listed.
allegations.key_passage: Here, we credit the Board’s explanation that it was not aware of the correspondence prior to the January 9 meeting and that it did not engage in discussion regarding the request, and we find that the Board did not violate the Open Meeting Law.

allegations.summary: Complainant alleged the Jan. 9, 2023 minutes failed to list a December 2022 letter and a January 7 email as documents used at the meeting.
allegations.key_passage: Merely mentioning that correspondence had taken place or referencing information from within a document does not render the document “used” such that they needed to be listed in the meeting minutes.

note: Read by a language model from the letter; every key passage is checked verbatim against it and dropped if not. A holding is the Attorney General’s reading of the law in this case only.
